info.title: Lenz — AI Fact-Checking API
info.description:
# Four API primitives for AI product teams

A research-depth ladder: find claims, judge them fast, prove them deep, follow up.

- `POST /extract` — enumerate every major verifiable claim in a document (up to 25, most check-worthy first, inputs to 50k chars); an optional `focus` narrows the list to the claims you care about. Costs no credits; fair-use cap 1,000/account/day.
- `POST /assess` — fast 3-model frontier panel verdict in ~5-10s. Sync, 1 credit.
- `POST /verify` — full 8-model pipeline with citations in ~90s. Async, 10 credits. Pass `depth: "low"` for a shallower check that comes back sooner — it costs the same, because depth caps research breadth and swaps no models.
- `POST /ask/{id}` — ask follow-up questions grounded on a verification.

## Built for teams whose AI output is async or document-shaped

Legal-memo generators, AI deep-research, due-diligence platforms, vertical agents producing structured deliverables, "report-as-a-service" companies. `/assess` opens the door to sync UX too — fast enough to gate a chat completion or a UI submit.

## Install the SDK

```bash
pip install lenz-io      # Python
npm install lenz-io      # Node / TypeScript
```

Source on GitHub: [lenz-io-python](https://github.com/lenzhq/lenz-io-python) · [lenz-io-node](https://github.com/lenzhq/lenz-io-node).

## The canonical integration: extract → assess → conditional verify

```python
from lenz_io import Lenz
client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")

# 1. Enumerate the factual claims in your model output (free)
# identified_claims is the complete ordered list when >1 claim is
# found (top claim included — iterate it alone); for a single claim
# it is [] and the claim lives in .claim.
# Pass focus="market size and competitors" to narrow the list;
# status is "no_match" when the document has claims but none match.
extracted = client.extract(text=llm_output)
claims = extracted.identified_claims or [extracted.claim]

# 2. Fast verdict on all of them via /assess (~5-10s, 3-model panel)
quick = client.assess(text=llm_output)

# 3. Escalate low-confidence claims to /verify (~90s, 8-model pipeline)
for c in quick.claims:
    if c.confidence == "low":
        deep = client.verify_and_wait(claim=c.claim)
        print(deep.verdict, deep.lenz_score, deep.key_finding)
```

## How /verify works under the hood

Frame → Collect Evidence → Debate (2 models, 2 rounds) → Adjudicate (3 models: sources, logic, precision) → Conclude. ~90 seconds wall-clock per claim.

### When /verify asks for input

`/verify` is not only submit-and-poll. `GET /verify/status/{task_id}` can terminate at `needs_input` — the submitted text held several claims, or was too vague to check as written — and the task waits rather than guessing which claim you meant.

Resolve it with `POST /verify/{task_id}/select`, passing the exact wording of the claim(s) you want from the ones the status offered. Selection is **by text, not index**; anything that was not offered is rejected with a 422. Each selected claim fans out into its own pipeline, so the response carries one `task_id` per claim — poll each the way you would a fresh `/verify`.

Claims returned by `/extract` skip this entirely: submitted verbatim, they are never bounced back for rephrasing.

### When /verify fails

A `failed` status (and the `verification.failed` webhook) carries two axes. `failure_reason` says **where** the pipeline stopped (`research_empty`, `conclusion_failed`, `task_stuck`, …). `failure_class` says **why**, and `retryable` is derived from it:

| `failure_class` | Meaning | `retryable` |
|---|---|---|
| `upstream_unavailable` | Model or search providers were rate-limited or down, or the task was never run — resubmit after a short wait | `true` |
| `insufficient_evidence` | We looked; the sources are not there | `false` |
| `invalid_input` | Not a checkable claim, an unresolvable ambiguity, an unreadable URL | `false` |
| `cancelled` | You stopped it | `false` |
| `internal` | Anything else — retrying the same input will not help | `false` |

Branch on `retryable`, not on `failure_reason`: the same reason can mean either. `failure_class` is a **closed set** — these five values are stable identifiers. `failure_reason` is an open, informational set (`task_error`, `task_stuck`, `not_a_claim`, … will appear). New keys may be added to status and webhook bodies without notice — ignore keys you do not recognise. A failed `/verify` is not charged.

## Common patterns

- **Runtime sync UX**: `POST /assess` on the user-facing path; escalate `confidence == "low"` claims to `/verify` in the background.
- **Runtime webhook**: `POST /verify` with `webhook_url`. Lenz POSTs the typed payload when done. Best for document pipelines.
- **CI / pre-release**: `/extract` + batch `/verify` your golden set on every deploy. The free `/extract` tier covers most of this. Claims returned by `/extract` verify cleanly — submitted verbatim to `/verify`, they are never bounced back for rephrasing.
- **Incident triage**: paste the offending output into `/extract`, then `/verify` the wrong-looking claims. Get a citation trail to send back to the customer.

## What's in the response

Unified vocabulary across every claim-shaped response:

- **`claim`** — the framed claim text.
- **`verdict`** — `"True" | "Mostly True" | "Mixed" | "Mostly False" | "False" | "Error"`.
- **`confidence`** — `"high" | "medium" | "low"`.
- **`lenz_score`** — 1–10 integer score (deep payloads).
- **`key_finding`** — one declarative sentence stating the most important fact the analysis established. For a false claim it states the CORRECTED fact rather than restating the claim, so render it next to the verdict label, never as a standalone headline. `""` on older verifications predating the field.
- **`sources`** — evidence with title, URL, snippet (`/verify` only).
- **`audit`** — adjudication reasoning, debate transcript, panel agreement (`/verify` only).

## How the API is organized

- **Extract** — pull verifiable claims out of text.
- **Assess** — fast 3-model verdict.
- **Verify** — deep 8-model pipeline: submit one claim or a batch, poll status, and resolve a `needs_input` interrupt by selecting claims.
- **Verifications** — list, fetch, delete, and toggle visibility on stored verifications.
- **Library** — browse the public catalog. No API key needed.
- **Ask** — follow-up questions, 1 credit each.
- **Account** — your credit balance and the price list.

## Credits

One pool per account funds every billable call, at a fixed weight:

| Endpoint | Credits |
|---|---|
| `POST /verify` (and `/verify/batch`, `/select`) | 10 per claim |
| `POST /assess` | 1 per claim |
| `POST /ask` | 1 |
| `POST /extract` | 0 — free, fair-use capped |

`GET /me/usage` reports the balance under `credits` and the weights under `costs`. The per-capability blocks beside them (`verify`, `assess`, `ask`) are **projections** of that one balance into each capability's own unit — how many of those calls the remaining credits would buy — not separate allowances. Spending on any one of them moves all of them.

## Authentication

1. [Create a Lenz account](https://lenz.io/auth).
2. Generate an API key on the [API credentials](https://lenz.io/api-credentials) page.
3. Send it on every request:
   ```
   Authorization: Bearer lenz_...
   ```

Or skip steps 1–2: **[lenz.io/setup](https://lenz.io/setup)** issues a test key and generates setup instructions for your environment — MCP client, SDK or plain HTTP — that you paste into your coding agent to do the wiring.

### One balance, whichever door you come through

Lenz also runs a remote MCP server at `https://lenz.io/mcp`, so an agent can fact-check inside a conversation. It is **not** part of this surface — there are no MCP endpoints below, and its tools are documented at [lenz.io/integrations/mcp-server](https://lenz.io/integrations/mcp-server).

It matters here for one reason: that server is a client of this API. It takes the same `lenz_...` key and forwards it to the endpoints below, so MCP traffic spends the same credits, counts against the same rate limits, and shows up in `GET /me/usage` — there is no separate MCP quota to check, and a 402 can just as easily be an agent as your own code.

## Idempotency

Send an `Idempotency-Key` header on `POST /extract`, `POST /assess`, `POST /verify`, and `POST /verify/batch` so retries after a network drop do not spawn duplicate tasks or double-debit quota. The server caches the response body and returns it on replay; a re-used key with a different body returns 422. The SDKs auto-generate a key per call by default.

## Errors

The status code says what to do next; the body says what happened. Every response carries an `X-Request-ID` header — quote it on a support ticket.

| Status | Condition | Retry? |
|---|---|---|
| 401 | Missing, malformed or unknown key | After fixing credentials |
| 402 | Out of credits, or the plan is the limit | No — billing action |
| 403 | Authenticated but not allowed (private verification, IP block) | No |
| 409 | An identical request is already in flight | Yes, shortly |
| 422 | Malformed input | No |
| 429 | Rate limit (the per-account `/extract` daily cap) | Yes, after `Retry-After` |
| 502 | A sync step (`/assess`, `/extract`) failed deterministically — a schema or parse failure | No — same input, same outcome |
| 503 | Our model providers were rate-limited or down for the step and every fallback was exhausted (`code: upstream_unavailable`), or the pipeline has no capacity (`code: capacity`) | Yes, after `Retry-After` (body `retry_after` too) |

**402** carries `detail`, `code` (always `no_credits`), `upgrade_url`, `doc_url`, `wall_id`, `cost` (what the rejected call would have taken), and — when resolvable — `remaining`, `credits_remaining` and `resets_at`. `remaining` and `requested` are in the *capability's* unit (verifications, assesses); `credits_remaining` and `cost` are in credits, so a client can tell "not enough for a 10-credit verify" from "empty". The resolvable fields are omitted rather than sent as `null`, so an absent key means "unknown", not "zero".

`wall_id` identifies this specific rejection and is already appended to `upgrade_url`, so sending a user to that URL is all that is needed — it exists as its own field only for clients that build their own upgrade link. Treat `upgrade_url` as opaque and follow it whole rather than matching it against a fixed string.

The `code` values are deliberately plan-agnostic: they name the condition, never the plan that would fix it. Send users to `upgrade_url` rather than mapping codes to plan names — the set of plans changes, the conditions do not.

An empty balance is deliberately **not** a 429: a 429 tells every client to retry, and an empty balance never succeeds on retry. **429** carries `code`, `limit`, `reset_in_seconds`, `upgrade_url` and the `Retry-After` header.

**Migrating (August 2026).** These rejections were 403, which the SDKs map to their auth error; they are now 402, which maps to the quota error — not a subclass. If you catch the auth error to handle an empty balance, that branch stops firing. This reaches you on every SDK version, including ones released before the change. `detail` strings are unchanged. Full reference: [lenz.io/docs/errors](https://lenz.io/docs/errors#quota).

## Webhooks

On `POST /verify` you may supply a `webhook_url`. We POST an HMAC-SHA256-signed JSON payload to it when the pipeline terminates. Signature header is `X-Lenz-Signature: sha256=<hex>`. Verify with your webhook secret (generate + rotate on [API credentials](https://lenz.io/api-credentials)). Retries: 10s, 60s, 600s (3 retries after the initial delivery, 4 attempts total). The SDKs ship a `LenzWebhooks` helper that verifies signatures and parses the payload into typed events.

For commercial use, volume pricing, or onboarding support, [get in touch](https://lenz.io/contact).

get.description:
Service discovery root — links to docs, OpenAPI spec, and endpoints.

Returned at ``GET /api/v1/`` so curious humans and probing clients
get a useful JSON payload instead of a 404.

Search and browse the public catalog of verified claims.

Returns paginated results from the Lenz Library. Only publicly
published verifications are included.

**Sort options:** `recent`, `most_true`, `most_untrue`,
`relevance` (only when `search` is provided), and `random`.

**`curated`** restricts results to one or more named curated collections,
comma-separated. Currently supported: `trivia` (the LLM-curated,
trivia-worthy pool behind the open-source quiz demo).

**`verdict`** filters to one or more verdict labels, comma-separated
(e.g. `True,False`). Labels: `True`, `Mostly True`, `Mixed`,
`Mostly False`, `False`.

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz()  # no api_key needed for the public library
page = client.library.list(page=1, sort="recent")
for v in page.items:
    print(v.claim, "→", v.verdict)

post.description:
Submit a claim for verification.

Returns a ``task_id`` immediately. Poll ``GET /verify/status/{task_id}``
or supply ``webhook_url`` in the body for an asynchronous callback when
the pipeline terminates.

**Duplicate submissions are collapsed.** With no ``Idempotency-Key``
header, the request body itself is the key: resubmitting an identical
body within 10 minutes returns the original ``task_id`` instead of
starting a second run. To run the same text twice on purpose, send your
own ``Idempotency-Key`` — a supplied key always wins.

**``depth``** selects how much research the check does. ``standard``
(default) is the full pipeline. ``low`` searches fewer sources and skips
the recovery fetch tiers, so it comes back sooner — with less evidence
behind the verdict. Every step runs the same models either way, and both
cost one unit of quota. The completed result echoes the depth the verdict
was actually produced with, which can read ``standard`` for a ``low``
request that was answered from an existing deeper check.

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
v = client.verify_and_wait(claim="Sharks don't get cancer")
# Add language="es" for Spanish output (12 languages supported).
# Add depth="low" for a shallower check that returns sooner.
print(v.verdict, v.lenz_score)
# false 2.0

post.description:
Fan-out wrapper around /verify for multi-claim LLM responses.

Body: ``{claims: [{text, source_url?, webhook_url?, visibility?, depth?},
...]}`` capped at 20 items. Server pre-checks total credits, then fans out N
independent pipelines — each with its own ``task_id`` and lifecycle.
Each claim's webhook (per-item override, or batch ``webhook_url``, or
per-key default) fires when its pipeline terminates. ``batch_id`` is
purely for client-side correlation; the server doesn't gate anything
on it.

On a mid-fan-out enqueue error, the response includes the partial
``items`` list and a ``partial: true`` flag. Per-claim credit spend
happens at each claim's normal persist time — claims that never
enqueue are never charged.

``depth`` works like ``visibility``: a batch-wide default that any item
can override. See ``POST /verify`` for what the values mean.

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
batch = client.verify_batch(claims=[
    {"text": "The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin."},
    {"text": "Water boils at 100°C at sea level."},
])
for item in batch.items:
    print(item.task_id, item.claim_text)

post.description:
Submit text for fast verdict via 3-model panel (sync).

Returns a per-atomic-claim verdict array in ~5-10 seconds. Cheaper
and faster than ``POST /verify``; uses 3 frontier models in
parallel and skips the research/debate/adjudication pipeline.

Smart-routed: time-sensitive claims (events from the past ~6
months) get a retrieval-grounded panel; evergreen claims get a
parametric panel.

Cache lookup chain: existing Claim row first (deep /verify
result), then Assessment row (prior /assess verdict). Both honor a
6h staleness rule for time-sensitive claims.

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
out = client.assess(text="Coffee causes cancer and the earth is flat.")
# Add language="es" for Spanish verdict text; verdict labels stay English.
for c in out.claims:
    print(c.claim, "→", c.verdict, c.confidence)

post.description:
Extract verifiable claims from arbitrary text.

Runs the standalone extraction step (`lenz.extraction`) — no research,
no debate, no credit charge. Enumerates every distinct major factual
claim in the input (up to 25), ordered most-check-worthy-first.
`identified_claims` is the complete ordered list when more than one
claim is found — iterate it alone; don't concatenate it with `claim`
(the top claim appears in both). Claims returned here verify cleanly
when submitted verbatim to `POST /verify`.

Pass `focus` to narrow the result to the claims you care about — a short
description such as `"market size, growth and competitors"`, at most 300
characters. A focus selects from the claims the extractor found and
nothing else: it cannot add a claim, reword one, reorder them, change the
language, or change what counts as a claim. Ordering stays
most-check-worthy-first.

`status` is one of:

- `ready` — claims were found (and, with a `focus`, at least one matched).
- `not_a_claim` — the input contains no verifiable factual claim at all.
- `no_match` — claims were found but none fall within your `focus`. The
  unfocused list is never substituted; widen the focus and call again.

Accepts up to 50,000 characters (longer input is truncated). Free for
API-key holders, capped at 1000 calls per ACCOUNT per day (resets at
00:00 UTC) regardless of input length — a focused call costs the same one
unit as an unfocused one. The cap is shared across all of the account's
keys. Keys with admin-set ``unlimited_extract=True`` bypass the cap.

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
claims = client.extract(text="Coffee causes cancer and the earth is flat.")
# Add language="es" to return extracted claims in Spanish.
for c in claims.identified_claims:
    print(c)

post.description:
Resolve a multi-claim / clarification interrupt by selecting one or more
of the offered claims.

Each selected claim fans out into its own independent pipeline (like
``/verify/batch``), so the response is batch-shaped:
``{batch_id, items: [{task_id, claim_text}], partial?}``. Poll each
``task_id`` via ``GET /verify/status/{task_id}``.

Every selected text must match a claim that was offered in the prior
``needs_input`` response (server-validated against the recorded offer set);
arbitrary client-asserted text is rejected.

get.description: Poll processing status for a submitted verification.

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
status = client.get_status("tsk_abc123")
print(status.status)  # "processing" | "needs_input" | "completed" | "failed"

get.description:
Return the calling account's credit balance and what it can still buy.

**``credits`` is the balance.** One pool funds every billable capability,
at the weights in ``costs`` — today ``verify`` 10, ``assess`` 1, ``ask`` 1.
It has two buckets: the monthly allowance for the current ``plan``, which
resets at ``resets_at``, and non-expiring ``bonus`` credits from grants and
top-ups, spent only once the allowance is gone. ``remaining`` is the sum,
and is what a call is actually checked against.

The per-capability blocks (``verify`` / ``ask`` / ``assess``) are
**projections** of that one pool into each capability's own unit —
"how many of these could I still make" — not separate allowances. Spending
on one moves all of them, and they are floor divisions, so a verify block
ticks once per 10 credits spent anywhere.

``bonus`` in each block is the bonus bucket in that capability's unit. The
older key ``credits`` is its deprecated alias, kept until 2026-11-29.

``extract`` is free at the pool (``costs.extract`` is 0) and is bounded by
a per-account daily fair-use cap instead, reported separately here and
rejected with 429 rather than 402.

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
u = client.usage()
# One credit pool funds every call; `costs` is the price list.
print(u.credits.remaining, "credits left", u.costs)
# The same balance, projected into one capability's unit.
print(u.verify.remaining, "verify calls left")
print(u.assess.remaining, "assess calls left")
print(u.credits.bonus, "of them non-expiring bonus credits")

get.description: List the authenticated key's verifications (all visibilities).

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
page = client.verifications.list(page=1)
for v in page.items:
    print(v.verification_id, v.verdict)

get.description:
Retrieve the full verification report for a single claim.

Returns the verdict, citations, and (under ``audit``) the panel
reasoning, debate transcript, and assessments. Same shape as the
/verify webhook payload and the deprecated /library/{id} endpoint
this merger replaces.

Authorization model (optional Bearer):
- Anon callers see any listed public claim (``visibility='public'`` AND
  ``status`` in {pending, published}) PLUS any API ``unlisted`` claim
  (``visibility='public'``, ``status='hidden'``, ``source_channel='api'``):
  unlisted is readable by verification_id, just never surfaced in listings.
- Authed callers additionally see their own claims regardless of
  visibility or status.
- Private claims, and non-API hidden public claims (retracted / pre-screen),
  owned by someone else return 404.

List public verifications semantically related to this one.

Returns the closest public-library claims by pgvector ANN distance
(cosine, 0 = identical). Excludes the verification itself, near-
duplicates (distance < 0.2), and editorially-hidden claims. Empty
list when the verification has no embedding yet (early pipeline) or
when no claim is close enough.

Authorization model (optional Bearer) — identical to
``get_verification``: anon callers reach listed public claims plus
API-origin unlisted ones; a valid key additionally unlocks the
caller's own claims. Results are always drawn from the public
library only, so keyless access exposes nothing new.
``limit`` is clamped to [1, 10].

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
related = client.verifications.related("vid_abc123", limit=5)
for r in related.items:
    print(r.verification_id, r.claim, r.verdict)

get.description: Get ask history and remaining quota for a verification.

delete.description: Delete all ask messages for this user on a verification.

post.description:
Send a question and get an expert response.

The reply (``content`` field on the response) is plain text with a
small markdown subset baked in by the chat model:

- ``**bold**`` and ``*italic*``
- ``- `` or ``* `` bullet lists
- Blank-line paragraph breaks; single newlines inside a paragraph
  mean line break

The model only produces these — no headings, no tables, no code
blocks. Pass the reply through any markdown library or display it
verbatim.

Documented at https://lenz.io/docs/quickstart#ask-reply-format.

EntityRef.description:
An entity (person, place, organization, concept) referenced in the
submitted claim.

``qid`` is the Wikidata Q identifier (e.g. ``Q42`` for Douglas Adams)
when Lenz resolved the entity against its internal catalog; ``null``
otherwise. Customers can join on ``qid`` to their own Wikidata-indexed
corpus, or hit the Wikidata API directly for richer metadata.
EntityRef.title: EntityRef

VerificationListItemOut.description:
Single item in a list of verifications.

Used by both ``GET /library`` (public catalog) and
``GET /verifications`` (authed-owner listing). Slim shape — no
``url`` (customers reference claims by ``verification_id``), no
``visibility`` (API claims are private by default; the field had
zero information value on the listing surface).
VerificationListItemOut.title: VerificationListItemOut

AssessClaimOut.description:
Per-claim entry inside an ``AssessOut.claims`` list.

Deliberately minimal — no model_votes, no panel identity, no
source/cache-provenance, no internal confidence label. The
``verification_url`` is the SDK's signal that a deep payload exists
for this claim; otherwise this row is the entire answer.

Same field vocabulary as ``ClaimDetailOut`` (``claim``, ``verdict``,
``confidence``); /assess just omits ``lenz_score`` (no deep score
is computed at this tier). ``language`` echoes the requested
output language so SDK consumers can route per-claim text in
batch responses where items may have different languages.
AssessClaimOut.title: AssessClaimOut

AssessOut.description:
Response body for ``POST /assess``.

``error_code`` is the machine-readable companion to ``error`` so callers
can distinguish a genuine non-claim (``'no_claim'``) from an ambiguous
claim that framing could disambiguate (``'ambiguous'``). For the ambiguous
case ``candidate_claims`` carries framing's specific readings so a caller
can pick one and re-assess — mirroring how ``/verify`` surfaces a
``clarification_required`` interrupt. Both fields are absent/empty on the
happy path; existing callers that only read ``claims``/``error`` are
unaffected.
AssessOut.title: AssessOut

ExtractOut.description:
The claims found in the submitted text.

`claim` is the most check-worthy claim. `identified_claims` is the
complete ordered list when more than one claim was found (the top claim
included — iterate it on its own) and `[]` for a single claim.

`status` is `ready` when claims were found, `not_a_claim` when the text
contains no verifiable factual claim, and `no_match` when a `focus` was
given and no claim falls within it.
ExtractOut.title: ExtractOut

text.description: The document to extract claims from. Up to 50,000 characters; longer input is truncated.
text.title: Text

language.description: ISO 639-1 code for the language of the emitted claims. Defaults to the input's language.
language.title: Language

focus.description: Optional. Narrows the result to the claims this describes, e.g. "market size, growth and competitors". At most 300 characters — a longer focus is rejected, never truncated. A focus can only select from the claims the extractor found: it cannot add a claim, reword one, reorder them, or change what counts as a claim. When nothing matches, `status` is `no_match` and `identified_claims` is empty; the unfocused list is never substituted.
focus.title: Focus

MeUsageCreditsOut.description:
The account's credit balance — the one pool every capability spends.

Two buckets: the monthly allowance for the current plan (resets at
``resets_at``) and non-expiring ``bonus`` credits from grants and top-ups,
which are spent only once the allowance is gone. ``remaining`` is the sum
and is what a call is checked against.
MeUsageCreditsOut.title: MeUsageCreditsOut

MeUsageExtractOut.title: MeUsageExtractOut

MeUsageOut.description:
The calling account's credit balance, and what it can still buy.

``credits`` is the balance and ``costs`` is the price list. The
``verify`` / ``ask`` / ``assess`` blocks are projections of that one pool
into each capability's unit — read whichever is convenient, but they all
describe the same money.

``extract`` is free at the pool (``costs.extract`` is 0) and carries a
per-account daily fair-use cap instead; it rejects with 429, not 402.
MeUsageOut.title: MeUsageOut

MeUsageQuotaOut.description:
One capability's share of the pool, projected into that capability's unit.

These are **projections, not allowances**. Every billable capability draws
on the single balance in ``MeUsageOut.credits``, at the weight in
``MeUsageOut.costs``; this block answers "how many ``/verify`` calls could
I still make if I spent everything on them". Spending on any capability
moves every block, and the division floors — a ``verify`` block whose
weight is 10 ticks once per 10 credits spent anywhere.

``bonus`` is the non-expiring bucket in this capability's unit.
``quota_used`` is derived as ``quota_total - quota_remaining``, so
``used + remaining == total`` always holds.

``credits`` is a DEPRECATED alias of ``bonus``, kept for compatibility
until 2026-11-29. It never meant the pool — before the pool existed it
meant this capability's one-off top-up balance, which is exactly what
``bonus`` now reports.
MeUsageQuotaOut.title: MeUsageQuotaOut

RelatedVerificationsOut.description:
Wrapper for ``GET /verifications/{id}/related``.

Empty ``items`` when the verification has no embedding yet (early
pipeline) or no public-library claim is close enough.
RelatedVerificationsOut.title: RelatedVerificationsOut

SimilarVerificationOut.description:
An existing public verification that semantically resembles a
given claim text.

Surfaced in two places:

* When duplicate detection finds a close-enough match on a fresh
  `/verify` (the ``duplicate_found`` needs-input branch).
* As an item in ``GET /verifications/{id}/related`` for callers
  surfacing "see also" references next to a verdict.
SimilarVerificationOut.title: SimilarVerificationOut

AssessmentOut.description:
An adjudicator's individual assessment. Nested under ``audit``.

``warnings`` carries the panelist-specific flags (logical fallacies for
the Logic Examiner, precision issues for the Precision Analyst, weakest
sources for the Source Auditor; verifications from before 2026-06 carry
missing context for the retired Context Analyst). The kind is implicit
in ``focus_area``; every panelist emits exactly one category.
AssessmentOut.title: AssessmentOut

AuditOut.description:
Audit / explainability block — for callers that need to show their work.

``panel_agreement`` is derived from the panel: ``unanimous`` (all agree),
``majority`` (score spread <= 2), or ``split``.
AuditOut.title: AuditOut

CandidateClaimOut.description:
A single candidate claim surfaced when the framing detects multiple
distinct claims in the submitted text. The caller picks one via
``POST /verify/{task_id}/select``.
CandidateClaimOut.title: CandidateClaimOut

ClaimDetailOut.description:
Full verification report.

Slim top-level (verdict + confidence + lenz_score + sources). Audit
detail (panel reasoning, debate, individual panelist assessments)
lives under ``audit``.

Same field vocabulary as ``VerificationListItemOut`` (list view) and
``AssessClaimOut`` (fast verdict). A consumer that branches on
``verdict`` or ``confidence`` reads the same field name regardless
of which endpoint produced the payload.
ClaimDetailOut.title: ClaimDetailOut

DebateSideOut.description: One side of the debate (pro or con). Nested under ``audit``.
DebateSideOut.title: DebateSideOut

NeedsInputOut.description:
Inline body for webhook ``event=verification.needs_input``.

The pipeline pauses for caller input when framing splits the text into
multiple distinct claims (``multi_claim``), needs disambiguation
(``clarification_required``), or finds a near-duplicate of an existing
verification (``duplicate_found``). Only one of ``claims``,
``candidates``, or ``similar_claims`` is populated per event, keyed
on ``reason``. Resolve by calling ``POST /verify/{task_id}/select``.
NeedsInputOut.title: NeedsInputOut

SourceOut.description:
A research source used to evaluate a claim.

``date`` is the source article's publication date (a source-level
attribute, not a Lenz API event time — so it's not renamed to
``published_at``).
SourceOut.title: SourceOut

WebhookPayload.description:
Body the customer's endpoint receives when a verification terminates.

Always signed with HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body bytes; signature
rides in the ``X-Lenz-Signature: sha256=<hex>`` header.

The ``attempt`` field is 1-indexed and includes the initial delivery,
so values run 1 through 4 (initial + 3 retries).
WebhookPayload.title: WebhookPayload
